Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Most students aren’t dating; everything here also fits friends, teams and family. Never make control a story about boys and girls only. If a student is worried about their own relationship, follow up privately and connect them with a counselor.

Every student in the room

Many students aren't dating and some are in relationships they keep private, including LGBTQ+ students; frame every pattern so it fits friendships, teams and families as well as partners, in relationships of every kind.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can tell healthy, unhealthy and abusive relationships apart, spot how control builds one small step at a time, and use three questions to check any relationship: a partner, a friend, a team, or family. Students who aren't dating should see the lesson fits them too.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minThumbs up, sideways or down?
  2. 5 minHow control builds, one step at a time
  3. 4 minHealthy, unhealthy, abusive
  4. 5 minOne in four, and the location question
  5. 12 minGreen, yellow or red? Ella, Theo, Nadia, Jordan
  6. 5 minWhy it’s hard to see from inside: turn and talk, share out
  7. 4 minThree questions that cut through it
  8. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The thumbs poll, how control builds, the three kinds, the location question, two of the four scenes, and the three questions.

Before you teach
Make the lesson fit students who aren't dating.

Say early: most of you aren't dating, and that's common. These patterns show up in friendships, teams and families too. That keeps everyone in the room engaged.

Some students are living this now.

Keep every example about the characters. Never ask anyone to describe their own relationship. The private self-check on the take-home page is where students can do that safely.

If a student says they're afraid.

Thank them, take it seriously, and walk them to a counselor that day. love is respect is free and confidential for young people: text LOVEIS to 22522.

Handle the self-harm threat carefully.

In the Jordan card, a partner threatens to hurt themselves. The answer: Jordan doesn't have to stay, tells a trusted adult, and points the partner to 988. Say it plainly and calmly.

Unhealthy can change. Abusive is different.

Keep the line clear. Unhealthy patterns can sometimes improve when both people work on them. Abuse is one person using control or fear, and trying harder won't fix it.

Expect the location-sharing debate.

Many students share location with friends and family. The test is whether they could turn it off without being punished, and whether it gets used to question them.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

LGBTQ+ relationships.

Use same-gender couples in examples alongside others. Threatening to out someone is a form of control. LGBTQ+ teens deserve the same help, and may have fewer adults they feel safe telling.

Every gender.

Boys can be on the receiving end of control and abuse and are often less likely to say so. Include "this only happens to girls" in the myths and answer it directly.

Family norms on location and phones.

In some families location sharing is simply expected, and parents check phones. Don't make that sound like abuse. The question is fear and punishment, not the app.

Private relationships.

Some students keep relationships hidden from family because of faith, culture or safety. Make clear that a counselor or a hotline can help without involving family first.

Family structure.

"Tell a trusted adult" might mean a grandparent, aunt, coach or older cousin. Let students choose.

Disability.

Students with disabilities can face control through help they rely on, like rides or devices. Mention that controlling someone's access to what they need is control too.

What the research says

About 1 in 12 high school students who dated in the past year experienced physical dating violence, and about 1 in 10 experienced sexual dating violence.

CDC, Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2021

Among teens with dating experience, 31% said a partner checked up on them several times a day, 21% had a partner read their texts without permission, and 13% had a partner demand their passwords.

Lenhart, Smith and Anderson, Pew Research Center, 2015

About 1 in 4 of 3,745 teens in relationships had experienced cyber dating abuse in the past year.

Zweig et al., Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 2013

5,681 teens tracked for about five years: those who experienced dating violence were more likely as young adults to have suicidal thoughts and to end up in violent relationships again.

Exner-Cortens, Eckenrode and Rothman, Pediatrics, 2013

In Massachusetts, people can seek an abuse prevention order against a dating partner, not only a spouse or family member.

Massachusetts General Laws c. 209A § 1

Since 2024, Massachusetts law counts coercive control (a pattern of threatening, isolating or controlling someone) as abuse when a person seeks a protective order.

Massachusetts General Laws c. 209A § 1, as amended by St. 2024, c. 118
